Stigmatized 'Jiko Bukken' Properties Draw Bargain Hunters in Japan Amid Rising Costs

29 Oct 2026, 06:36 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Business Desk · Source: www.bbc.co.uk

Japan's real estate market features a distinct category of homes known as jiko bukken, or "stigmatized" properties, where suicides, murders, deaths by fire, or unattended lonely deaths have occurred. While cultural aversions to these locations traditionally drove down their market value significantly, rising living costs and surging house prices have led a growing number of unfazed buyers and renters to snap them up at steep discounts.

Regulations and Disclosure Rules

Under official guidelines issued by the Japanese government in 2021, estate agents are legally required to disclose specific tragic events that occurred within a dwelling. For rental units, this disclosure mandate applies for three years following the incident. However, for properties offered for sale, the requirement to reveal such history remains indefinite.

These regulations stand in contrast to practices in other nations. For instance, the UK has no legal obligation to disclose if a person has died in a property. In the United States, disclosure requirements vary by state; California mandates revealing deaths within the past three years, whereas states like Arizona and Oregon have no such requirement.

Financial Incentives for Unfazed Buyers

The cultural weight attached to yuurei—the concept of lingering, troubled spirits of people who died in violent, tragic, or lonely circumstances—means these properties are often difficult to sell or rent through conventional channels. Consequently, those willing to overlook the stigma can secure substantial financial savings.

In Tokyo's fashionable Setagaya ward, a young entertainer known as Ryua secured an approximate 30% discount on a tiny 25-square-meter bedsit where a previous occupant took his own life. She pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) monthly instead of the standard 62,000 yen rate, noting that she experiences daily paranormal occurrences like footsteps and talking.

Similarly, in rural Kagoshima in Japan's southwest, 79-year-old American resident Diane Tincher purchased a large three-bedroom house for roughly half the typical asking price—paying 20 million yen instead of the usual 45 million yen—because an elderly resident had previously died alone there.

Practical Implications and Market Shifts

For readers evaluating the Japanese property market or examining international real estate comparisons, several factors are confirmed by available reports:

  • Confirmed vs. Unknown: It is confirmed that Japanese law requires specific disclosures for rentals (three years) and sales (indefinitely) regarding suicides, murders, fires, and extended undiscovered deaths. It is also documented that crowd-sourced platforms like Oshimaland track these locations. The internal personal experiences of occupants regarding ghosts remain subjective and unverified.
  • Market Trends: Driven by surging house prices and a higher cost of living, a 2025 survey indicated that more than half of Japanese people would now consider renting a jiko bukken if the price was sufficiently low.
  • Verification: Readers can review the original reporting and verify official disclosures through the BBC News report at https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy78elyrlzo.
